fiirsy:275: Another fundamental problem with traditional R&D documentation is that it is written and maintained by humans. If we treat documentation as a special kind of "code"—code can be generated, modified, and verified by Agents, and so can documentation. When an Agent modifies an API implementation, it can update the API docs at the same time; when an Agent refactors a piece of business logic, it can update the architecture description; when an Agent fixes a bug, it can automatically record it in the changelog. Documentation is no longer an accessory to code, but a first-class citizen that is version-controlled, reviewed, and verified by automated tests alongside code.

q69fw6:369: Traditional release processes are a typical scenario where Agent capabilities are systematically limited. From code commit to production deployment, the entire pipeline is full of approval gates, manual verification steps, and breakpoint-style collaboration designed for humans. Agents can generate code and run tests, but cannot directly trigger builds; if the build passes tests, they cannot automatically deploy to staging; if staging verification passes, they cannot push to production. Permissions are distributed across different systems and roles, and every step requires human intervention. The deeper problem is the lack of transparency in the release process. CI logs, test reports, performance metrics, and canary data are scattered across different systems, with no unified interface for Agents to access programmatically. When a release fails, an Agent cannot automatically analyze the cause, roll back, or retry—it can only wait for human handling. A true Agent-oriented release process should make Agents participants rather than bystanders: automatically triggering builds, deploying, monitoring, and adjusting canary distribution or rolling back according to preset rules. Humans shift from process executors to rule-makers and exception handlers.
